[Model and example](../vignettes/03_transition_model/03_transition_model.ipynb) · [All benchmarks](../benchmark.qmd)

The pass-selection model gives the probability of each candidate destination, conditional on a pass attempt. A shared XGBoost ensemble produces a utility for every destination, and a softmax turns the utilities into a categorical choice distribution. We also evaluate an exploratory cross-nested logit (CNL) that groups destinations probabilistically by potential receiver. The [model vignette](../vignettes/03_transition_model/03_transition_model.ipynb) introduces the choice model, its predictors and an executable example. The likelihood-based tree learning follows [RUMBoost](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trc.2024.104897).

## Evaluation cohort

The evaluation uses the **same pass attempts as the pass success probability task**: **6,810 decisions across ten SkillCorner matches**, of which **1,009 are unsuccessful passes**. Passers are outfield players. Unsuccessful passes are kept because destination choice is defined independently of completion. The observed endpoint is assigned to the nearest cell centre of the one-metre pitch grid, and all candidate cells enter the categorical normalization. The pooled uniform-choice reference cross entropy is **8.873286**.

## Features

The model uses 19 numerical predictors and two one-hot encoded contextual variables (50 encoded columns). They cover pass geometry, raw target pitch control, expected threat, pressure-line indices, one-second ball-drive loss, game context and player counts beyond the carrier and target lines; definitions are in the [model vignette](../vignettes/03_transition_model/03_transition_model.ipynb). All predictors are built from information available at the decision frame, so the observed receiver and the subsequent outcome are excluded. Pitch control enters in its raw form, without isotonic calibration.

## Choice specifications and learning

For decision $i$, let $\mathcal G_i$ be the candidate destination cells, $y_i$ the observed destination and $z_{ij}$ the features of cell $j$. Both specifications use **one shared XGBoost ensemble**, $u_{ij}=f_\theta(z_{ij})$, to score all alternatives. They differ in the map from utilities to probabilities, and therefore in the derivatives used to fit the ensemble.

### Flat multinomial logit

The deployed specification applies a softmax:

$$
p_{ij}=\frac{\exp(u_{ij})}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal G_i}\exp(u_{ik})}.
$$

The ensemble minimizes the categorical negative log-likelihood

$$
\mathcal L=-\sum_i\log p_{i,y_i},
$$

with utility gradient $g_{ij}=p_{ij}-\mathbf 1\{j=y_i\}$. This is a **single categorical likelihood over destinations**: the probability of each cell depends on the utilities of all cells in the same decision, so cells are never treated as independent binary outcomes.

### Exploratory cross-nested logit

The CNL keeps the same utility function and lets each destination belong fractionally to several **receiver nests**, one per eligible teammate other than the carrier. Membership $\alpha_{ijm}$ is proportional to teammate $m$'s **individual raw pitch control** at destination $j$, normalized over eligible teammates (a zero-control destination gets uniform membership). Memberships are fixed by the physical state and are not estimated with the trees.

With $\rho=1/\mu$, define

$$
S_{im}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal G_i}(\alpha_{ijm}e^{u_{ij}})^\rho,
\qquad
p_{ij}=\sum_m
\underbrace{\frac{S_{im}^{1/\rho}}{\sum_l S_{il}^{1/\rho}}}_{\text{nest probability}}
\underbrace{\frac{(\alpha_{ijm}e^{u_{ij}})^\rho}{S_{im}}}_{\text{destination within nest}}.
$$

A single dissimilarity parameter $\mu\in[0.1,1]$ ($\rho\in[1,10]$) is shared by all nests, because teammate identities and nest compositions change from decision to decision and teammate-specific scales would not be comparable. **At $\mu=1$ the CNL reduces to the flat softmax.** For $\mu<1$ it relaxes the independence-of-irrelevant-alternatives restriction of the flat model, allowing more structured substitution among destinations tied to the same receiver.

Both models minimize the **same observed-choice negative log-likelihood**. For the CNL, probabilities, gradients and curvature are computed from the CNL probability function. In both cases XGBoost receives one gradient and one scalar curvature per candidate.

### Iterative XGBoost estimation

The estimation follows [RUMBoost](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trc.2024.104897), adapted to XGBoost and a single shared utility ensemble (the RUMBoost reference implementation uses LightGBM). The same ensemble $f_\theta$ is evaluated on every candidate, so no separate predictor is fitted per destination. Tree construction and regularization follow [Chen and Guestrin (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02754). Ensembles start from zero utilities, and the CNL also starts at $\mu=1$.

At boosting iteration $t$, the current utilities $u_{ij}^{(t)}$ define a full probability distribution over the destinations of each pass. The loss of the observed choice, $\ell_i=-\log p_{i,y_i}$, gives the direction in which utilities should move: alternatives with too much probability receive positive gradients, and the chosen destination receives a negative gradient in the flat model.

XGBoost adds a regression tree $b_t$ that minimizes a local quadratic approximation of the loss, built from $g_{ij}=\partial\ell_i/\partial u_{ij}$ and the curvature $h_{ij}$. With leaf outputs $w_A$,

$$
\widetilde{\mathcal L}_t(b_t)=
\sum_{i,j}\left[g_{ij}b_t(z_{ij})+\frac12 h_{ij}b_t(z_{ij})^2\right]
+\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_A w_A^2.
$$

For a leaf $A$, let $G_A=\sum_{(i,j)\in A}g_{ij}$ and $H_A=\sum_{(i,j)\in A}h_{ij}$ aggregate the candidate rows assigned to it. The optimal leaf output is

$$
w_A^*=-\frac{G_A}{H_A+\lambda}.
$$

The tree is grown to maximize the reduction of this objective, subject to the depth and minimum-child-curvature constraints. Its output is added to the **utility function shared by all destinations**, with learning rate $\eta$:

$$
u_{ij}^{(t+1)}=u_{ij}^{(t)}+\eta\,b_t(z_{ij}).
$$

Because the update changes the probabilities of *all* destinations in a pass, gradients and curvatures are recomputed from the new categorical distributions before the next tree. This repeated re-evaluation of the choice likelihood is what links discrete-choice estimation to gradient boosting.

**Curvature convention.** The exact categorical Hessian has off-diagonal terms linking alternatives of the same pass, whereas XGBoost takes one scalar per row. For the flat softmax the implemented convention is

$$
\boxed{\displaystyle
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\partial^2\ell_i}{\partial u_{ij}^2}=p_{ij}(1-p_{ij}),\qquad
\frac{\partial^2\ell_i}{\partial u_{ij}\partial u_{ik}}=-p_{ij}p_{ik}\quad(j\neq k),\\[5pt]
h_{ij}^{\mathrm{flat}}=\max\!\left\{\varepsilon,\frac{J_i}{J_i-1}p_{ij}(1-p_{ij})\right\},
\qquad J_i=|\mathcal G_i|.
\end{gathered}}
$$

The factor $J_i/(J_i-1)$ follows the [RUMBoost reference implementation](https://github.com/big-ucl/rumboost/blob/v1.0.2/rumboost/rumboost.py), and $\varepsilon$ keeps the curvature away from zero. For the CNL, **gradient and scalar curvature both come from the CNL likelihood**. The two models therefore share the boosting machinery and optimize different probability maps. The scalar curvature is a tree-fitting approximation and does not assume statistical independence among candidate destinations.

**Dissimilarity update.** The CNL learns $\mu$ together with the trees. After every 20 trees, the utilities are held fixed and the categorical likelihood is minimized over $\rho\in[1,10]$ with bounded SLSQP. Only 10% of the proposed move is applied, to avoid abrupt changes in the choice probabilities:

$$
\rho^{(t+1)}=\rho^{(t)}+0.1\bigl(\rho^*-\rho^{(t)}\bigr).
$$

Boosting then resumes with probabilities and derivatives recomputed at the new dissimilarity. Validation cross entropy selects the joint checkpoint of tree ensemble and $\mu$. This alternating scheme extends the [RUMBoost cross-nested approach](https://transp-or.epfl.ch/heart/2024/abstracts/hEART_2024_paper_8384.pdf) to fixed pitch-control memberships and the shared PRESS XGBoost utility.

## Model selection and validation

### Hyperparameter screening

Before the held-out evaluation, **five hyperparameter configurations** were compared for each model family on **one development partition**: six matches for training and two for validation. The partition was the same for flat and CNL, and the remaining two matches were left out of screening. The criterion was validation cross entropy. The screening was limited and did not cover the full hyperparameter space.

| Maximum depth | Minimum child weight | L2 | Flat | CNL |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 6 | 5 | 3 | 5.808242 | **5.774532** |
| 3 | 5 | 1 | 5.808396 | 5.800588 |
| 4 | 20 | 1 | **5.800526** | 5.775927 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 5.818136 | 5.794084 |
| 4 | 5 | 1 | 5.819215 | 5.794499 |

The lowest validation cross entropy selects **depth 4, `min_child_weight` 20, L2 1** for the flat model and **depth 6, `min_child_weight` 5, L2 3** for the CNL. Both use learning rate 0.05, row and column subsampling 0.8, CPU histogram boosting, at most 2,000 trees and early-stopping patience 100. These settings were **fixed before** the five-fold evaluation. Since the selected capacities differ, a performance gap cannot be attributed to nesting alone.

### Match-wise held-out evaluation

The selected configurations were evaluated on **five match-disjoint 6 + 2 + 2 partitions**:

- **Six training matches** fit the XGBoost utilities and the upstream feature components (physical pass-risk and ball-drive parameters, xT smoothing, categorical vocabulary).
- **Two validation matches** select the tree checkpoint by early stopping, then fit a **single temperature-scaling parameter** with the trees held fixed. They contribute no training examples to the trees.
- **Two test matches** are used only for performance evaluation and determine neither the number of trees nor the temperature.

Each of the 6,810 decisions appears exactly once among the pooled test predictions. Upstream physical fitting and calibration are documented in the [pass-probability benchmark](02_pass_probability.qmd) and [ball-drive benchmark](01_ball_drive_risk.qmd). The full-data deployment refit is described at the end.

## Predictive performance

Pooled held-out results over the five partitions, with each family's screening-selected hyperparameters:

| Model | Calibration | Cross entropy | McFadden $R^2$ |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Flat | Raw | 5.828043 | 34.319% |
| Flat | Temperature | **5.827787** | **34.322%** |
| CNL | Raw | 5.816478 | 34.450% |
| CNL | Temperature | **5.810553** | **34.516%** |

Relative to the calibrated flat model, the calibrated CNL lowers cross entropy by **0.017234** and raises McFadden $R^2$ by **0.194 percentage points**. Eight of ten match-level cross entropies favor the CNL. The calibrated fixed-prediction match-bootstrap contrast excludes zero; this is descriptive, since it does not account for repeated model development and selection. The observed advantage is small and does not establish a substantial practical benefit of nesting.

| Fold | Flat trees | CNL trees | CNL $\mu$ | Flat $T$ | CNL $T$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1,408 | 359 | 0.5770 | 1.0169 | 1.0607 |
| 1 | 1,444 | 399 | 0.5892 | 1.0170 | 1.0766 |
| 2 | 1,491 | 375 | 0.5514 | 0.9889 | 1.0342 |
| 3 | 1,527 | 359 | 0.6015 | 1.0069 | 1.0538 |
| 4 | 1,213 | 319 | 0.6253 | 1.0037 | 1.0524 |

All fits stopped before the tree ceiling. Given the modest CNL gain and its added structural and optimization complexity, **the flat model is retained for deployment** and the CNL is kept as an exploratory alternative. This result does not show that nesting is unhelpful in general.

A possible explanation for the limited gain is that pass geometry, raw pitch control and the other contextual predictors already give the nonlinear utility model an informative representation of destination choice. This is a **hypothesis**. It is neither an identified causal mechanism nor proof that nesting is unnecessary on other data.

## Comparison with published results

| Study / model | Cross entropy ↓ | McFadden $R^2$ ↑ |
|---|---:|---:|
| **PRESS, flat + temperature scaling** | **5.827787** | **34.322%** |
| Fernández et al. (2021), SoccerMap | 5.7134 | ≈35.543% |

[Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (2021)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10994-021-05989-6) report a pass-selection cross entropy of **5.7134** (Table 4). The McFadden value shown here is **derived** from that figure with a uniform $104\times68$ choice grid and is not a published metric. Their fully convolutional SoccerMap model was evaluated on a different dataset (**633 matches**), open-play cohort, split and candidate-grid construction. The comparison gives **context and no like-for-like ranking**, and the gap cannot be attributed to model architecture alone.

## Final fitted model and scope

After evaluation, the flat model was refitted on all ten matches with **1,444 trees** (the median validation-selected count across folds) and no further hyperparameter optimization. The deployment model uses full-data physical feature fits and smoothed xT. Its temperature, **$T=1.0132954379$**, was estimated from reconstructed raw out-of-fold distributions and is not a new held-out evaluation. The installed artifact is `skillcorner_outfield_pass_selection_flat_v3`. The CNL full-data refit (359 trees, $\mu=0.6263079567$, $T=1.0558986079$) is kept for research and is not deployed by default.

The ten matches were examined repeatedly during development, and hyperparameters came from a common exploratory screening without fully nested optimization. The results are therefore a development-stage comparison and no independent confirmation. The number of candidate cells does not increase the number of independent decisions or matches.

For reproducibility, the [screening table](../data/benchmarks/pass_selection/screening54.csv), [pooled metrics](../data/benchmarks/pass_selection/final_pooled_metrics.csv), [fold summaries](../data/benchmarks/pass_selection/final_fold_summary.csv), [per-match results](../data/benchmarks/pass_selection/final_metrics_by_match.csv) and [installed artifact provenance](../docs/pass-selection-final-provenance.json) are provided as supplementary resources.
